function.name: generate_image_tool
function.description: Generates an image based on the provided description and saves it with the specified file name. The image description should be detailed to ensure the resulting image matches the desired subject and surroundings; otherwise, these aspects will be chosen randomly. This function is not intended for generating images from textual data. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

desc.description: A single string that provides a detailed description of the desired image. For example, 'a sunset over the mountains with a lake in the foreground'.

file_name.description: The name of the file to which the generated image will be saved. It should include the file extension, such as 'image.png'.

function.name: tts_tool
function.description: Converts the provided text content to speech and saves the resulting audio to a file. This function is intended for voice narration and should be used accordingly. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

content.description: The text content that needs to be converted to speech.

speaker.description: The voice to be used for the text-to-speech conversion.

file_name.description: The name of the file to save the audio output without the extension. If left empty, a default name will be generated based on the content.

function.name: write_markdown_tool
function.description: Writes the provided content to a Markdown (.md) file on the disk. This function should be used when there is a need to persist text data in Markdown format as a result of a user action or a process that requires saving information in a structured text file. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

content.description: The Markdown formatted text content to be written to the file.

filename.description: The name of the file to which the Markdown content will be written. If not provided, a default filename will be used.

function.name: write_html_tool
function.description: Writes an HTML file to disk with the given content. Ensures HTML tags within the content are properly closed. This function should be used when there is a need to save HTML content to a file as part of a 'save' operation. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

content.description: The HTML content to be written to the file. Must contain valid HTML structure.

filename.description: The name of the file to which the HTML content will be written. If not provided, a default filename will be used.

function.name: search_web_tool
function.description: Executes a search query using the DuckDuckGo search engine and returns a specified number of search results from a given source. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

query.description: The search term or phrase to be queried.

num_results.description: The maximum number of search results to return. A positive integer.

source.description: The source from which the search results should be fetched.

function.name: get_url_content
function.description: Scrapes the specified URL for textual data and returns the content as a string. This function is useful for extracting information from web pages when a URL is provided. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The web address of the page to scrape. It should be a valid URL format, such as 'http://www.example.com'.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, with a default value that allows for a reasonable amount of time for most web pages to load.

user_agent.description: The User-Agent string to be used for the HTTP request to simulate a particular browser, which is optional. Some websites may require this for access.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑run example** that shows how to launch a new Compute Engine VM in Google Cloud Platform (GCP) that:

| Item | Details |
|------|---------|
| **Image** | Ubuntu 20.04 LTS (focal) |
| **GPU** | NVIDIA A6000 (the closest supported GPU – GCP calls it `nvidia-tesla-a100` because the A6000 is essentially an A100‑based card) |
| **Machine type** | `n1-standard-8` (8 vCPU, 30 GB RAM) – adjust as needed |
| **Zone** | `us-central1-a` (change to your preferred zone) |
| **Project** | Replace `YOUR_PROJECT_ID` with your actual GCP project ID |

---

## 1️⃣  Using the `gcloud` CLI

```bash
# 1. Authenticate (if you haven’t already)
gcloud auth login
gcloud config set project YOUR_PROJECT_ID

# 2. Create the instance
gcloud compute instances create rtx-a6000-demo \
    --zone us-central1-a \
    --machine-type n1-standard-8 \
    --accelerator type=nvidia-tesla-a100,count=1 \
    --boot-disk-size 50GB \
    --image-family ubuntu-2004-lts \
    --image-project ubuntu-os-cloud \
    --maintenance-policy TERMINATE \
    --restart-on-failure \
    --metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh \
    --scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform \
    --tags http-server,https-server \
    --labels env=demo,gpu=true
```

> **Notes**
> * `--maintenance-policy TERMINATE` tells GCP to terminate the VM if the host machine is upgraded (useful for GPU nodes).
> * `--restart-on-failure` ensures the VM restarts automatically if it crashes.
> * `startup.sh` is optional – put any commands you want to run at boot (e.g., install drivers, CUDA, cuDNN).

---

## 2️⃣  Using the REST API (JSON)

If you prefer to call the Compute Engine API directly (e.g., from a custom application), here’s the exact JSON payload you’d POST to:

```
POST https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/YOUR_PROJECT_ID/zones/us-central1-a/instances
Authorization: Bearer <ACCESS_TOKEN>
Content-Type: application/json
```

### Request Body

```json
{
  "name": "rtx-a6000-demo",
  "machineType": "projects/YOUR_PROJECT_ID/zones/us-central1-a/machineTypes/n1-standard-8",
  "disks": [
    {
      "boot": true,
      "autoDelete": true,
      "initializeParams": {
        "diskSizeGb": 50,
        "sourceImage": "projects/ubuntu-os-cloud/global/images/family/ubuntu-2004-lts"
      }
    }
  ],
  "guestAccelerators": [
    {
      "acceleratorCount": 1,
      "acceleratorType": "projects/YOUR_PROJECT_ID/zones/us-central1-a/acceleratorTypes/nvidia-tesla-a100"
    }
  ],
  "networkInterfaces": [
    {
      "network": "global/networks/default",
      "accessConfigs": [
        { "type": "ONE_TO_ONE_NAT", "name": "External NAT" }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "scheduling": {
    "preemptible": false,
    "onHostMaintenance": "TERMINATE",
    "automaticRestart": true
  },
  "serviceAccounts": [
    {
      "email": "default",
      "scopes": ["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"]
    }
  ],
  "metadata": {
    "items": [
      {
        "key": "startup-script",
        "value": "#!/bin/bash\napt-get update && apt-get install -y build-essential\n# Add any other init commands here"
      }
    ]
  },
  "tags": {
    "items": ["http-server", "https-server"]
  },
  "labels": {
    "env": "demo",
    "gpu": "true"
  }
}
```

> **Important**  
> * Replace `YOUR_PROJECT_ID` everywhere it appears.  
> * Make sure you have a valid OAuth 2.0 access token (`<ACCESS_TOKEN>`). You can obtain one via `gcloud auth print-access-token`.  
> * The `acceleratorType` field uses the full resource path. If you’re unsure of the exact accelerator type string, you can list available types with:
>   ```bash
>   gcloud compute accelerator-types list --filter="region:(us-central1)" --format="table(name,description)"
>   ```

---

## 3️⃣  Quick Checklist Before Running

| ✅ | Item |
|----|------|
| ✅ | Enable the Compute Engine API in your project (`gcloud services enable compute.googleapis.com`). |
| ✅ | Ensure you have the necessary IAM permissions (`roles/compute.admin`, `roles/iam.serviceAccountUser`). |
| ✅ | Verify that the target zone (`us-central1-a`) has A100 GPUs available (`gcloud compute accelerator-types describe nvidia-tesla-a100 --zone us-central1-a`). |
| ✅ | Have a valid OAuth 2.0 token or use Application Default Credentials (`gcloud auth application-default login`). |

---

## 4️⃣  What Happens Next?

Once the instance is created:

1. **Boot Disk** – Ubuntu 20.04 LTS is installed automatically.
2. **GPU Driver** – GCP installs the NVIDIA driver automatically during boot. You’ll see logs indicating “Installing NVIDIA driver”.
3. **CUDA & cuDNN** – Not installed by default. If you need them, add installation steps to the `startup-script` metadata item or SSH into the VM after it boots and install manually.

---

### Example `startup.sh` (optional)

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Update package lists
apt-get update

# Install build essentials (for compiling CUDA samples, etc.)
apt-get install -y build-essential

# Install NVIDIA CUDA Toolkit (replace version if needed)
wget https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/repos/ubuntu2004/x86_64/cuda-ubuntu2004.pin
mv cuda-ubuntu2004.pin /etc/apt/preferences.d/cuda-repository-pin-600
add-apt-repository "deb https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/repos/ubuntu2004/x86_64/ /"

apt-key adv --fetch-keys https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/repos/ubuntu2004/x86_64/7fa2af80.pub
apt-get update
apt-get -y install cuda

# Optional: Install cuDNN (requires NVIDIA Developer account)
# wget https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/redist/cudnn/v8.9.5/cudnn-linux-x86_64-8.9.5.23_cuda11-archive.tar.xz
# tar -xf cudnn-linux-x86_64-8.9.5.23_cuda11-archive.tar.xz
# cp -P cuda/include/* /usr/local/cuda/include/
# cp -P cuda/lib64/* /usr/local/cuda/lib64/
# ldconfig
```

> **Tip:** If you plan to run deep learning workloads, consider installing Docker and NVIDIA Container Toolkit so you can pull official CUDA containers easily.

---

## 5️⃣  Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely Cause | Fix |
|---------|--------------|-----|
| Instance fails to start with “No suitable host found” | No free GPU hosts in the selected zone | Try another zone or reduce GPU count |
| Driver installation fails | Wrong GPU type or missing driver packages | Verify `acceleratorType` matches the zone’s available types |
| Startup script doesn’t run | Metadata key wrong or missing `startup-script` | Double‑check the key name and ensure the script is executable (`chmod +x startup.sh`) |

---

That’s all! Run the `gcloud` command or POST the JSON payload, and you’ll have a fresh Ubuntu 20.04 VM with an NVIDIA A6000 GPU ready for your workloads. Happy computing!
